name: Chrome and OS defenses against notification abuse
plain: Browser rules that quiet, throttle and auto-revoke abusive notification sites.
meaning: Shows how the browser limits what an ignored or abusive site can do: a quiet prompt chip, auto-revocation, server-side throttling at FCM. A site that is ignored keeps no permission and sends nothing.

web.api: n/a (browser policy, Safety Hub, FCM throttling)

access.prompt_ui: Quiet prompt chip, Notifications blocked message in the address bar, Safety Hub revocation list, Android one-tap unsubscribe.
access.persistence: Revoked permissions can be re-granted from Safety Hub
access.revocation: Safety Hub, Site settings, notification Unsubscribe action
steps: Chrome decides to show quiet UI based on past allow rate and abuse signals
Chrome revokes after low engagement or repeated warnings
FCM throttles domains above 1,000 messages per minute and returns HTTP 429

fields.name: Auto-revoke escalation
fields.precision: back to normal after about 42 days (secondary source)

limits.headline: Can't keep sending spam if you block it; Chrome quiets and removes abusers
limits.user_action: You ignore the prompt, tap Block, or tap Unsubscribe on a notification
can: Show a quiet chip instead of a loud pop up for sites people rarely allow
Remove permission for sites you have not used in a while
Let you review removed sites in Safety Hub, or unsubscribe with one tap on Android
cannot: Send anything after you block it or it is auto removed
Send notifications from a site you never allowed
Use a big pop up on every visit for a site that you ignored
Skip these checks in Chrome, Edge or Firefox
limits.reach_label: Limits what a site can do
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Firefox have these protections. Safari and iPhone browsers use different rules.

story.what_it_is: Browser rules that quiet, limit and switch off notification permissions from sites that spam you.

marketing.name: Quieter notification permissions
marketing.pitch: Chrome shows a quieter prompt and can auto remove permissions from sites that send unwanted alerts.

story.for_you: You may see a small quiet icon instead of a big prompt. Chrome may also remove permissions from sites you never use. You get fewer pop ups and fewer spam alerts.
story.for_makers: Makers must earn permission by asking at the right moment and sending useful alerts. Spammy sites lose permission automatically. Browsers use this to keep notifications trusted.

use_cases.example: A news site that asks for permission on first page load gets quiet prompts, so it waits to ask after a reader reads two articles.
A store that sends too many promos sees low opt in and users turning alerts off.
Fake virus warning sites that abused alerts for scams lose permission and show fewer pop ups.
A browser game portal sends one useful alert for a turn ready, instead of daily nags that cause blocks.
A social site tests asking after a user follows an account, not at once, to keep its permission rate high.
A push ad network sees reduced reach as browsers block spam and remove stale permissions.
A company dashboard sends few, high value alerts to keep permission across staff browsers.

technical_bounds: Cannot be opted out of by the site
Installed PWAs keep access in Chrome
Numbers other than the FCM limit come from secondary sources
